extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students learning proof techniques (proof by contradiction)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for constructing and writing proofs by contradiction, including logical foundations, typical proof structure, common patterns (e.g., 'no smallest X', irrationality proofs), and cautionary advice about when to use the method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure of a proof by contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: When proving a statement P by contradiction, assume its negation (∼P) and show that this assumption leads to a contradiction. Use a chain of implications (∼P ⇒ P1 ⇒ P2 ⇒ ... ⇒ Pn ⇒ CONTRADICTION) and then reason backwards via modus tollens to conclude (∼P) is false and hence P is true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the generic template: explicitly state 'We will prove this by contradiction'; assume (∼P); derive a chain of implications that terminates in an always-false statement (e.g. R ∧ (∼R)); conclude (∼P) is false and therefore P true. The write-up should present this neatly as a standard proof-by-contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tell the reader you are using contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Alert the reader that the proof is by contradiction so the next step (assuming the negation) does not look like a mistake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin with a phrase such as 'We will prove this by contradiction' or 'Assume, to the contrary...' to be kind to the reader and clarify proof strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious about when to use contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Proof by contradiction is a tool among many; do not use it by default for every proof. Try a direct or contrapositive proof first because they have clearer start and end points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warning (11.0.1 / 11.1.1): contradiction proofs can be harder to aim because the target contradiction is not always obvious. Use contradiction after exploring direct/contrapositive approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose an effective contradiction to aim for
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide what false statement you will derive (e.g. Q ∧ (∼Q), an arithmetic impossibility, a divisibility contradiction), and plan the chain of implications to reach it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One common approach is, when (∼P) requires introducing some witness Q, aim to later derive (∼Q). Another pattern: for 'no smallest' results aim to construct a strictly smaller example (X1 and X2 with X2 < X1) to get Q ∧ (∼Q).

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard pattern for 'no smallest / no largest' proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove statements like 'There is no smallest (or largest) X', assume such an X1 exists and construct a different X2 that contradicts minimality (e.g. produce r/2 < r).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example (Result 11.1.2): assume smallest positive real r exists, then r/2 is a smaller positive real, yielding contradiction r is both smallest and not smallest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of logical principles: law of excluded middle and modus tollens
rubrics_metrics.description: Proof-by-contradiction relies on the law of excluded middle (P ∨ ∼P) and modus tollens: from (P ⇒ Q) and ∼Q infer ∼P.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about the logical move: deriving a contradiction shows ∼P is false via the law of excluded middle; use modus tollens to move backward along implication chains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negate quantified and implication statements carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: When negating quantified/implicative statements, apply quantifier and implication negation rules correctly (e.g. ∼(∀x, Q(x) ⇒ R(x)) ≡ ∃x such that Q(x) ∧ ∼R(x)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work with quantifiers explicitly in scratchwork to produce the correct starting assumptions for a contradiction-proof and state them clearly in the write-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: When proving an implication via contradiction, assume a counterexample (witness)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove ∀x ∈ S, Q(x) ⇒ R(x) by contradiction, assume there exists x ∈ S with Q(x) true and R(x) false and derive a contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start by asserting existence of that witness (from the negation) and proceed to contradict other known facts; remind reader you are using contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irrationality-proof strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a number is irrational by contradiction, assume it is rational and thus can be written as a ratio a/b of integers; then deduce that this forces the number to have a property contradictory to the assumption (e.g. both numerator and denominator even).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example (√2): assume √2 = a/b with a,b integers having no common factor; deduce both a and b are even which contradicts coprimality. General guidance: aim to show the assumed irrational is actually rational (or vice versa).

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose rational representations in lowest terms and check denominators
rubrics_metrics.description: When assuming rational representations, take numerator and denominator coprime (remove common factors) and explicitly verify denominators are non-zero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text emphasizes that if q = c/d with gcd(c,d)>1 you may reduce to a/b with gcd(a,b)=1; in write-up, state this reduction and check b ≠ 0 (and similarly for other fractions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use parity / divisibility lemmas for integer contradictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Common integer contradictions use facts like 'n^2 is even iff n is even' or divisibility arguments to show impossible divisibility (e.g. 2 divisible by 4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply earlier lemmas (referenced Lemma 5.1.5 style facts) to link squares/parity to divisibility, then derive contradictions about common factors or impossible divisibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Euclid-style contradiction for infinitude of primes
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume finitely many primes p1,...,pr, form N = p1 p2 ... pr, consider N+1 and show it yields a contradiction (N+1 is a new prime or has a prime divisor absent from list).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work the two cases (N+1 prime vs composite) and show both contradict the assumption that the list contained all primes; present as a clean contradiction proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write up proofs neatly and be explicit to aid the reader
rubrics_metrics.description: When converting scratchwork to final proof, write the logical structure clearly, warn the reader about method, and display key steps (e.g., show denominators non-zero, state when you've reduced to coprime integers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors repeatedly advise being 'kind to your reader': explicitly state assumptions, method, and check technical conditions rather than leaving them implicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and correct common faulty contradiction arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Be alert to fallacies such as assuming a universal negation incorrectly or concluding irrationality from absence of a particular representation without proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example of a faulty proof is given for 'if x,y irrational then xy irrational' — such blanket statements require counterexamples or rigorous proof; use counterexamples to disprove false universal claims.
